problems.memo_sentence: The authors explicitly target four stylized facts—non‑Gaussianity, absence of linear autocorrelation, volatility clustering, and leverage effect—as properties that generated series should match.
problems.source_evidence: “The QGANs that we trained generate synthetic financial time series that not only match the target distribution but also exhibit the desired temporal correlations, with the quality of each property depending on the hyperparameters and simulation method.” / “the quality of each property depending on the hyperparameters and simulation method.” / “the QGAN using the PQC given in figure 2 shows the closest match of this property … whereas … adding a CNOT gate … increases the absolute autocorrelation … and using CZ gates instead … causes a quicker decrease of this effect.”
problems.explanation: The memo states the target facts as if they are simply the paper’s objectives, but it omits the paper’s explicit limitation that the quality of reproducing these facts depends on hyperparameters and simulation method. That caveat is central to the results and discussion.

problems.memo_sentence: Using full‑state simulation, the trained QGAN produces S&P 500‑like time series that closely match the target return distribution, exhibit no linear autocorrelation, and show weaker but decaying absolute autocorrelation and leverage effects, indicating partial recovery of volatility clustering and leverage.
problems.source_evidence: “The QGAN using the PQC given in figure 2 shows the closest match of this property … whereas PQC architectures where an additional CNOT gate is added at the end of each layer leads to an increase in the absolute autocorrelation for higher time lags … and using CZ gates instead of CNOT gates in the PQC causes a quicker decrease of this effect.” / “The three simulations performed with the full-state simulation show different behavior in particular of the absolute autocorrelation of the generated time series, indicating different qualities in capturing volatility clustering.”
problems.explanation: The memo presents the full-state result as a general success, but the paper emphasizes that the temporal-correlation quality varies substantially across full-state architectures and that the chosen architecture is only the closest match. This architectural sensitivity is a key limitation that the memo does not reflect.

problems.memo_sentence: For the MPS approach, fidelity of the tensor‑network approximation improves with bond dimension and can become numerically indistinguishable from full‑state simulation at sufficiently high bond dimension, enabling training of deeper circuits than feasible with full‑state simulation, though the temporal effects in the generated series are weaker than in the full‑state case; circuit depth increases entanglement and reduces MPS fidelity at fixed bond dimension.
problems.source_evidence: “For higher bond dimensions and number of layers, the training time in the MPS simulation increases, and the stylized facts of the generated time series vary considerably for each choice of the number of layers and bond dimension.” / “the training of QGANs with PQCs of a higher number of layers and qubits and MPS of higher bond dimensions increases the number of epochs needed in the training. Additionally, each training epoch takes a longer time for these more complex models.”
problems.explanation: The memo captures the fidelity trend but omits the paper’s explicit scalability limitation: higher bond dimension and more layers substantially increase training time and epochs needed. That practical cost is part of the paper’s main caveat about MPS.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the theoretical status of any learning or expressivity separation for their expectation‑value‑sampler QGAN is explicitly stated as an open question, so potential quantum advantage is speculative.
problems.source_evidence: “It remains an open question if such separations can also hold for estimation value sampler as we use here.” / “However, even without separations it may be the case that quantum models simply have more convenient inductive biases than classical models and understanding those is valuable”
problems.explanation: The memo mentions the open question, but it understates the paper’s broader caution: the paper does not claim a quantum advantage, only possible inductive biases. This is a limitation on the interpretation of the work that should be reflected more explicitly.
